ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology Referral — Ronald Reagan — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit one month after right hip fracture repair, with dementia and caregiver assessment

text.paragraph: Moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 90-year-old man one month after a fall at home and repair of a right hip fracture. Please confirm the stage, review whether donepezil is still worthwhile given his heart rate and fall risk, and advise on mild evening restlessness without antipsychotics. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care check. [S]

list.item: Do you agree that his dementia is at the moderate stage (FAST stage 5)?
Is donepezil still giving benefit, and is it safe to continue with a heart rate in the low 60s and a recent fall?
How should the evening restlessness and repeated questions be managed without antipsychotics or sedatives?
Would you add memantine now, and is any further testing needed?

text.paragraph: Alzheimer's disease diagnosed many years ago, on donepezil 10 mg each morning. Before the fracture he walked independently but needed help choosing clothes and with all instrumental activities of daily living (Lawton IADL 1 of 8), consistent with FAST stage 5. Today MoCA 11 of 30, GDS-15 4, and Confusion Assessment Method negative for delirium. NPI-Q shows mild evening restlessness and repeated questions, with no hallucinations or aggression. Heart rate 64 with no orthostatic drop (128/70 seated, 124/70 standing); Timed Up and Go 24 seconds with a front-wheeled walker and standby help. TSH 2.3. The hospital oxycodone and diphenhydramine were stopped today; scheduled acetaminophen and enoxaparin to day 35 continue, and vitamin D was started for a level of 16 ng/mL. His caregivers' Zarit Burden Interview score is 41 of 88, and caregiver support is being arranged [S]

list.item: His spouse is afraid he will fall again, especially at night, and is exhausted. [S]
He wants to walk outdoors in the garden again and to stay at home. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Ronald Reagan was born on February 6, 1911, in Tampico, Illinois, to Jack and Nelle Reagan; his older brother Neil was born in 1908. [D]

In a letter to the American people made public on November 5, 1994, Reagan wrote that he had recently been told he was one of the millions of Americans who would be afflicted with Alzheimer's disease, and that as the disease progresses the family often bears a heavy burden. [D]

Reagan's personal physicians stated in November 1994 that his annual examinations included memory testing, that over the preceding twelve months they had seen findings suggesting possible early Alzheimer's disease, and that after further testing and observation they concluded he was entering its early stages. [D]

Reagan was thrown from a horse in Mexico on July 4, 1989; at a routine examination at the Mayo Clinic in September 1989, doctors found fluid on his brain attributed to the fall, and it was removed surgically at St. Mary's Hospital in Rochester, Minnesota. [D]

Reagan fell at home on January 12, 2001, and broke his right hip; the next day, at St. John's Health Center in Santa Monica, surgeons repaired it with a pin, plate, and screws in a 65-minute operation. He went home on January 20, 2001, and continued physical therapy at home, with no weight-bearing sessions for at least two weeks. [D]
Reagan survived an assassination attempt in 1981, had an operation for colon cancer in 1985, and had prostate and skin-cancer surgery in 1987. [D]
Reagan's father, Jack, died of a heart attack on May 18, 1941, and his brother, Neil, died of heart failure on December 11, 1996. [D]
Reagan's mother, Nelle, died on July 25, 1962, of complications of Alzheimer's disease, according to the Reagan Library. [D]

Stop oxycodone and diphenhydramine, keep acetaminophen scheduled, and finish 35 days of enoxaparin; review every medicine against the AGS Beers Criteria at each visit. Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline (2021); American Geriatrics Society 2023 updated AGS Beers Criteria for potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Home physical and occupational therapy, a home safety assessment, and a CDC STEADI fall-risk check at every visit. Guideline: Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Replete vitamin D, aim for 1,000 to 1,200 mg of calcium a day from food, then obtain DXA and give intravenous zoledronic acid at about three months once calcium and kidney function are checked. Guideline: The clinician's guide to prevention and treatment of osteoporosis (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Monitor dementia on the CMID schedule: yearly MoCA, FAST stage, and ADL and IADL scores; neuropsychiatric screen and depression screen at follow-up. Guideline: Alzheimer's Association clinical practice guideline for the Diagnostic Evaluation, Testing, Counseling, and Disclosure of Suspected Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders (DETeCD-ADRD) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Support the caregiver: Zarit Burden Interview at the first and six-month visits, weekly respite, a home health aide, caregiver education, and Alzheimer's Association support services. Guideline: Alzheimer's Association clinical practice guideline for the Diagnostic Evaluation, Testing, Counseling, and Disclosure of Suspected Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders (DETeCD-ADRD) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]

Advance care planning with the patient and spouse: confirm the health care agent, discuss goals of care, and complete a POLST form; revisit at each change in stage. Guideline: Alzheimer's Association clinical practice guideline for the Diagnostic Evaluation, Testing, Counseling, and Disclosure of Suspected Alzheimer's Disease and Related Disorders (DETeCD-ADRD) (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Alzheimer's disease, hip/pelvic fracture, and osteoporosis monographs (2026) [S]
